Information in the December 13, 2017 FOMC statement conveys a constructive macro backdrop—“solid” growth and a “strong” labor market—paired with below-target inflation and a 25 bp rate hike to 1.25–1.50%. The Committee’s emphasis on “gradual” increases is consistent with inertial, forward-looking policy rules and flexible inflation targeting that balance real activity against a symmetric 2% objective. Implementation via interest on reserves and ON RRP, plus continued balance-sheet normalization, supports a transparent, rule-like operating framework. Two dovish dissents underscore concern over persistent sub-2% inflation even as policy remains accommodative and below longer-run neutral.

SLOOS overlay (October 2017) tempers the outlook:
- Business credit supply: Banks eased standards for C&I loans (competition-driven), a modest positive for capex financing.
- Consumer credit conditions: Banks tightened terms for credit card and auto loans, citing loan portfolio quality, collateral values, supervisory/legislative/accounting considerations, and capital/liquidity positions—pressuring consumer credit availability.
- Loan demand: Banks reported weakened demand for credit cards and auto loans, and softer business demand tied to inventory, accounts receivable, plant/equipment investment, and M&A—pointing to cooler momentum in both household spending and investment.
- Offsets: Banks maintained willingness to make consumer installment loans.

Net takeaway: While the macro data in the FOMC statement is upbeat and policy guidance remains gradual, SLOOS signals tighter consumer credit, cautious risk appetite, and softer loan demand across several uses, slightly dampening the growth/inflation impulse and reinforcing a cautiously hawkish but more measured tone for financial conditions.
